steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing TRAM, a fine-tuning optimizer that combines sharpness-aware minimization with trust region regularization for out-of-distribution generalization. Motivate it from flat minima and the pre-train/fine-tune paradigm, contrast the two smoothing perspectives, and end with a bulleted contributions list.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Training a neural model means navigating a complex, non-convex loss surface to get to a good local minimum. Studying loss surfaces and training dynamics has led to many algorithmic advances and to regularization schemes that improve optimization. One of these strategies uses a link between generalization and flat minima, which were defined in earlier work as “region[s] in weight space with the property that each weight vector from that region has [a] similar small error”. The intuition is that a flatter, or less sharp, minimum generalizes better, because the loss function will not increase under distribution shift. Recent work developed a family of sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) algorithms that target flat minima by minimizing a worst-case generalization bound and local parameter sharpness together.

Flat minima methods report improvements over conventional optimizers in many settings, but we argue that they are not fully connected to the modern fine-tuning paradigm, where a task-specific model inherits its parameters from a pre-trained model instead of being trained from scratch. In this setting, focusing on local properties of the loss landscape (e.g., sharpness) may fail because it does not make good use of the useful generic task-agnostic structures in pre-trained representations. In this work we propose to combine sharpness-aware minimization with robust transfer of pre-trained information (in representation space) for fine-tuning scenarios that need out-of-distribution knowledge to adapt successfully.

- Representation smoothing vs parameter smoothness
  - existing ways to leverage pre-trained structure: trust region regularization (cite), adversarial perturbation (cite)
  - focus on function curvature: smooth local changes in representations
  - lower representation curvature limits catastrophic forgetting (cite) of pre-training information
  - contrasts with SAM parameter smoothness; both improve downstream tasks (cite); fusion under-explored

- TRAM and contributions
  - TRAM: Trust Region Aware Minimization; fine-tuning for out-of-distribution generalization; sharpness-aware + trust region
  - trust region bound informs SAM adversarial neighborhood; function-curvature awareness for flatter minima
  - low-sharpness parameters, better adaptation of pre-trained models; focus on distribution transfer in Transformer-based models
  - contribution 1: new algorithm; multiple variants (trust region estimation, efficiency trade-offs) (Section 3)
  - contribution 2: better generalization across vision and language: cross-dataset image classification, cross-domain language modeling, zero-shot cross-lingual transfer (Section 4)
  - contribution 3: analysis - limits catastrophic forgetting, flatter minima; major/minor shifts, anticorrelated scenarios; smoother loss surface in- and out-of-domain; better representation similarity seen/unseen distributions (Section 4)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Training a neural model means navigating a complex, non-convex loss surface to get to a good local minimum. Studying loss surfaces and training dynamics has led to many algorithmic advances and to regularization schemes that improve optimization. One of these strategies uses a link between generalization and flat minima, which were defined in earlier work as “region[s] in weight space with the property that each weight vector from that region has [a] similar small error”. The intuition is that a flatter, or less sharp, minimum generalizes better, because the loss function will not increase under distribution shift. Recent work developed a family of sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) algorithms that target flat minima by minimizing a worst-case generalization bound and local parameter sharpness together.

Flat minima methods report improvements over conventional optimizers in many settings, but we argue that they are not fully connected to the modern fine-tuning paradigm, where a task-specific model inherits its parameters from a pre-trained model instead of being trained from scratch. In this setting, focusing on local properties of the loss landscape (e.g., sharpness) may fail because it does not make good use of the useful generic task-agnostic structures in pre-trained representations. In this work we propose to combine sharpness-aware minimization with robust transfer of pre-trained information (in representation space) for fine-tuning scenarios that need out-of-distribution knowledge to adapt successfully.

There are existing methods to make better use of pre-trained structure during fine-tuning, such as trust region regularization or adversarial perturbation. These methods look at the curvature of the function itself, e.g., by encouraging smooth local changes in representations. The intuition is that if the representation curvature is lower during fine-tuning, the function is less likely to catastrophically forget useful information from pre-training. This representation smoothing approach is different from SAM-style optimization for parameter smoothness. Both perspectives improve results in downstream tasks empirically, but combining these strategies has not been explored much yet.

So we propose TRAM: Trust Region Aware Minimization, a fine-tuning algorithm for out-of-distribution generalization that combines sharpness-aware and trust region optimization. TRAM uses a trust region bound to inform the SAM adversarial neighborhood, which brings awareness of function curvature into the optimization for flatter minima. The algorithm gives low-sharpness parameters and better adaptation of pre-trained models to downstream tasks. To show that TRAM is better than strong baselines at keeping generic representations, we focus on distribution transfer challenges in Transformer-based models. Our contributions are:

- We propose a new optimization algorithm, Trust Region Aware Minimization, which puts representation smoothing regularization into sharpness-aware minimization. We propose and compare several variants of TRAM based on different perspectives on trust region estimation and on efficiency trade-offs (Section 3).

- We show that TRAM empirically improves generalization on several out-of-distribution adaptation tasks in vision and natural language: cross-dataset adaptation for image classification, cross-domain language modeling and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer (Section 4).

- We analyze how TRAM limits catastrophic forgetting and optimizes flatter minima to improve fine-tuning. By looking at major and minor distribution shifts, we find that TRAM does better than the trend in anticorrelated generalization scenarios. Our analysis shows that TRAM optimizes a smoother loss surface for both in-domain and out-of-domain distributions. TRAM also improves the representation similarity between seen and unseen distributions, which improves cross-domain classification (Section 4).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Neural model training requires navigating a complex, non-convex loss surface [1] towards a good local minimum. Studying loss surfaces and training dynamics has led to many algorithmic advances [2,3,4] and regularization schemes [5,6] that improve optimization. One such strategy exploits an association between generalization and flat minima, defined by [7] as “region[s] in weight space with the property that each weight vector from that region has [a] similar small error”. Intuitively, a flatter, or less sharp [8], minimum should generalize better, since the loss function will be non-increasing under distribution shift. Recent work has developed a family of sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) algorithms that target flat minima by jointly minimizing a worst-case generalization bound and local parameter sharpness [3,9,10,11].

While flat minima methods report widespread improvement over conventional optimizers [12], we argue that they are not fully connected to the modern fine-tuning paradigm, in which a task-specific model inherits parameters from a pre-trained model instead of being trained from scratch [13,14]. In these settings, focusing on local properties of the loss landscape (e.g., sharpness) may fail by suboptimally exploiting the useful generic task-agnostic structures within pre-trained representations. In this work, we propose combining sharpness-aware minimization with the robust transfer of pre-trained information (in representation space) for fine-tuning scenarios that require out-of-distribution knowledge for successful adaptation.

Existing methods for better leveraging pre-trained structure during fine-tuning include trust region regularization [15,16,17] and adversarial perturbation [18,19]. These methods focus on the curvature of the function itself, e.g., by encouraging smooth local changes in representations. The intuition is that lower representation curvature during fine-tuning keeps a function from catastrophically forgetting [20] useful information from pre-training. This representation smoothing approach contrasts with SAM-style optimization for parameter smoothness. Both perspectives show empirical improvements on downstream tasks [17,21], but a fusion of the two strategies is currently under-explored.

To this end, we propose TRAM: Trust Region Aware Minimization, a fine-tuning algorithm for out-of-distribution generalization that combines the success of sharpness-aware and trust region optimization. TRAM uses a trust region bound to inform the SAM adversarial neighborhood, introducing an awareness of function curvature into optimization for flatter minima. The resulting algorithm yields low-sharpness parameters and improved adaptation of pre-trained models to downstream tasks. To illustrate TRAM's advantage over strong baselines in retaining generic representations, we focus on distribution transfer challenges in Transformer-based models. Our contributions are:

- • We propose a new optimization algorithm: Trust Region Aware Minimization integrates representation smoothing regularization into sharpness-aware minimization. We propose and contrast multiple variants of TRAM based on different perspectives on trust region estimation and on efficiency trade-offs (Section 3).

- • We show that TRAM empirically improves generalization for multiple out-of-distribution adaptation tasks across vision and natural language: cross-dataset adaptation for image classification, cross-domain language modeling and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer (Section 4).

- • We analyze how TRAM limits catastrophic forgetting and optimizes flatter minima to improve fine-tuning. By characterizing major and minor distribution shifts, we identify how TRAM outperforms the trend in anticorrelated generalization scenarios. Our analysis verifies that TRAM optimizes a smoother loss surface for both in-domain and out-of-domain distributions. TRAM also improves representation similarity between seen and unseen distributions, which improves cross-domain classification (Section 4).
